Phase contributions

Phase 1 — Quantum Kernel PrescreenCompares each event with normal behaviour.
Phase 2 — Quantum AutoencoderLearns normal signals and flags what it cannot rebuild.
Phase 3 — QAOA SelectorPicks the most suspicious events as a group.
Each phase gives a score per row. The model combines the scores into one score per row with tuned weights per dataset, and flags a row when that score is at or above the operating threshold. The weights are held by Copenhagen Quantum.

Tuning results per dataset

Still tuning · runs paused 13 Nov 07:27 for a software update ·

Each study runs as three independent repeats and needs 400 counted trials per repeat to finish. A counted trial is one the study accepts towards that total. No study has finished. All runs were paused on 13 November at 07:27 for a software update and will continue from the levels shown here, so every number below is still tuning: a best-so-far validation result, not a final result.

How to read these results

  • Still tuning. No study has finished. Every number in this table is the level reached when the runs were paused on 13 November: best-so-far validation results, not final results and not test results.
  • Compare every score with its base rate. The score is average precision. Guessing at random already scores about the share of anomalies in the data.
  • OTDR Event Classes has 87.25% anomalies (125,832 rows). Its average precision has a baseline near 0.87. A score of 0.87 there means almost no skill, not "87% performance". The score shown comes from its re-run with corrected inputs (31 measured features), which had finished only 4–5 trials per repeat when paused.
  • Acoustic Sensing: Field Events has very few anomalies, at most 1 validation anomaly per repeat. One event changes the score a lot, so treat it as a rough indication.
  • Acoustic Sensing: Audible Signals has 10 anomalies in the development data. The same caution applies.
  • This table shows version 2.7 only. The replay, matrix and score tile at the top of the page show one recorded version 2.6 run; the two versions are not mixed in either place.

Subsea: ships over a seabed cable

Preliminary · public dataset Marlinks-NS (Zenodo 15611778, CC BY 4.0) · not GlobalConnect data

DAS on a 28 km seabed telecom cable off Zeebrugge, Belgium, 16–25 June 2023. Choose "Ships over a subsea cable" in the dataset menu at the top for the full data description and the numbered anomaly classes.

What counts as an anomaly

  • Anomaly: a 10-second window with a vessel within 1,000 m of the cable. Ship traffic over a subsea cable is the main source of anchor and fishing-gear damage.
  • What a ship looks like in the signal: engine and propeller tones in the tens of Hz, strongest at the sensing points nearest the ship, moving along the cable as the ship passes. Large ships are louder and lower in pitch; small boats are weaker and only picked up close by.
  • Normal: sea and seabed noise, and distant shipping.

→

How to read this

  • All rows: ship within 1,000 m, scored once on the 3 held-out days (23–25 June, 22,009 windows, 7,012 with a ship). Small numbers under ROC-AUC: 95% range from a block bootstrap over the held-out days.
  • Average precision is compared with 0.319, the share of held-out windows with a ship, which is what random guessing scores.
  • Ships caught at 1% / 5% false alarms: the share of ship windows flagged when the alarm level is set so that 1% / 5% of the held-out windows without a ship are flagged.
  • QAD 2.7.9 and 2.7.10 give the same numbers in every digit, default and tuned. Each was tuned separately from its default settings and both tunes picked the same setting; 2.7.10 changes speed and robustness, not the model's maths.
  • On this dataset QAD is below the best classical methods: Mahalanobis distance 0.931 and the tuned isolation forest 0.927, against 0.912 for QAD. QAD is above the one-class SVM. The ranges overlap, so the gap is not settled by one short tune.

How to read this

  • Share of each class's ship windows flagged at the alarm level that gives 5% false alarms on the held-out windows without a ship. QAD 2.7.9 gives the same numbers as 2.7.10.
  • Large ships are caught far more often than small ones: 89% of windows with a ship of 250 m or more, 21% with a ship under 50 m. Hopper dredgers are the hardest type (33%).
  • T6 general cargo ships (333 windows), T8 LPG tankers (318) and T9 other types (797) were not broken out in this run.

Possible unregistered vessels (class "b") Preliminary, unconfirmed

A "b" detection is a ship-like DAS signal while AIS reports no vessel within 1,000 m of the cable. The detector is the QAD 2.7.10 release candidate as tuned above on the "a" ships. Its alarm levels were set on 21–22 June, and it was run once on the 61.1 held-out hours (23–25 June).

Alarm levelWindows flagged with no AIS vessel within 1 kmNearest AIS vessel 1–2 km2–5 kmOver 5 kmExpected from false alarms aloneMoving ship-like source beyond 2 km (candidates)
1% false alarms2361517510about 1500
5% false alarms91866222630about 750229 windows, 4.8 minutes, 0.13% of the held-out hours

What this shows

  • Headline: at the 1% level, no candidate. At the 5% level, 2 candidates. In both, AIS reports a chemical/oil products tanker of about 185 m at 3.6–4.7 km, so that tanker is the more likely source. So there is no clear sign of an unregistered vessel in these 3 days, but the test is strict and misses many real ships (see below).
  • Why the candidates count only beyond 2 km: large ships are heard well beyond 1 km, so flags with an AIS vessel 1–2 km away most likely come from that ship.
  • Flags in total: 1.6% of the windows with no AIS vessel within 1 km are flagged at the 1% level, against 1% expected from false alarms alone. Most flags are single windows or have a peak that does not move along the cable.
  • No window is free of ships: every window has some AIS vessel within 9.2 km.
  • The moving-source test is strict: it passes only about 30% of flagged runs from real AIS ships within 1 km. It cannot follow a ship crossing the cable at a right angle, and it places the source only to within 194 m.
  • Size and type of a candidate cannot be read reliably yet. A classical model trained on the "a" ships reads the length band above chance for ships within 1 km (balanced accuracy 0.54; chance 0.25), but it recognises almost no vessels under 50 m and drops to 0.34 at 1–2 km. Type: 0.31 against 0.20 by chance.
  • No candidate can be confirmed: this dataset has no radar or satellite data.

Read with care

  • Preliminary: a short tune on one public dataset, not a finished study.
  • Only ships that broadcast AIS are labelled. A nearby ship without AIS counts as normal.
  • The data contains ships passing, not anchor drags or cable damage.
  • The waters off Zeebrugge are among the busiest in Europe, so ships near the cable may not be rare. The share of ship windows is shown with the results.

Anomaly types

What each dataset covers · public research data, not GlobalConnect data

Each box is one family of anomaly that matters for a fibre network. It lists the event types in our datasets that fall under it, how they were sensed, and whether the anomalies are real recordings or simulated. The last box lists what no dataset here covers yet.

1 · Works and activity near the route

Activity close to a buried cable, accidental or staged.

Fibre Intrusion

  • Dig — digging in the soil above or beside the buried cable; the pattern behind excavation damage, the most common cause of cable cuts on land.
  • Walk — a person walking above the cable: regular footstep impacts, usually harmless but easy to confuse with digging.
  • Water — water poured onto the ground above the cable: a weak, spread-out vibration.

Acoustic Sensing: Field Events

  • Construction — construction work near the route.
  • Car — a car driving past the route.
  • Running and walk — people running or walking near the route.
  • Longboard — a longboard rolling along the route: continuous rolling vibration.

TerrestrialReal Φ-OTDR and DAS vibration

2 · Direct contact with cable plant

Someone touching, handling or opening the cable or its enclosures.

Fibre Intrusion

  • Knock — knocking on the ground or the cable cover: short, sharp impacts.
  • Shake — shaking the cable or its surroundings by hand: direct mechanical handling.

Acoustic Sensing: Field Events

  • Manipulation — handling of the cable itself.
  • Open/close — opening and closing near the route, such as a door or an enclosure.
  • Fence — activity at a fence along the route.

TerrestrialReal Φ-OTDR and DAS vibration

3 · Sound aimed at the fibre

Acoustic sources picked up by the fibre acting as a long microphone.

Acoustic Sensing: Audible Signals

  • Continuous frequency sweep — a tone gliding across the audible range.
  • Stepped frequency sweep — a tone stepping from one frequency to the next, at normal, raised and quieter levels.
  • Speech test signal (STIPA) — a standard speech-like signal, a stand-in for people talking near the cable, at the same three levels.

TerrestrialReal DAS, audible band

4 · Fibre and link faults

Faults in the fibre itself, seen in the light it reflects.

Fibre Health Simulated

  • Reflective fault — a sharp reflection at one point, as from a dirty or loose connector, an air gap or a clean break, added to a simulated access-network trace.

OTDR Event Classes Real

  • Seven event classes — reflective events (connectors, breaks), non-reflective events (splices, bends), events lying so close together they merge, and fault sub-categories. The source numbers the classes without naming each one.

Terrestrial Fibre Health · Route type not stated OTDR Event Classes · OTDR traces

5 · Ships over a subsea cable

A vessel within 1 km of a seabed cable, a proxy for anchor and fishing-gear risk.

Marlinks-NS (public, CC BY 4.0)

  • Ship within 1,000 m — engine and propeller tones picked up by a 28 km seabed cable off Zeebrugge, over 10 days in June 2023.
  • By ship type — container ships, Ro-Ro cargo ships, chemical and oil products tankers, hopper dredgers, vehicle carriers, general cargo ships, bulk carriers, LPG tankers, and other types, from ship-tracking (AIS) data.
  • By ship length — under 50 m, 50–150 m, 150–250 m, 250 m and over, and not reported: larger ships are louder and heard from further away.
  • Possible unregistered vessel — a ship-like signal with no AIS vessel within 1,000 m. Preliminary result: no clear candidate in the 3 held-out days.

SubseaPreliminary DAS on a subsea cable · see its section

Not covered yet

  • Anchor drag or fishing gear actually striking a subsea cable
  • A cable cut or break recorded on a live link
  • Fibre tapping by bending the fibre
  • Slow degradation, such as ageing or rising splice loss
  • Polarisation-based sensing: a public subsea polarisation dataset is downloaded but not yet analysed

Phase 4 — IBM QPU Validation

Validation plan · v0.1 · 2026-11-09

The planned real-hardware step: tuned circuits run on a real superconducting IBM Heron processor (ibm_fez, 156 qubits), and the scoring is compared against NumPy, ideal Aer and noise-modelled Aer. The real QPU step has not run for any dataset. The levels below describe the plan and its pass rules.

QPU vs HPC validation
—
Not yet measured
Aer ↔ NumPy gate
—
Real-QPU dispatch
—
PASS threshold
ρ ≥ 0.85
5% drift tolerance vs HPC reference
LEVEL A · NumPy
Classical reference
The final configuration runs on NumPy. This sets the reference scoring and the PR-AUC headline. No quantum hardware involved.
LEVEL B · Aer ideal
Noise-free simulator
The same circuits on the Qiskit Aer noise-free simulator. Expected to match NumPy closely (Spearman ≥ 0.99). Gate: ρ(NumPy, Aer) ≥ 0.90. A failure blocks the QPU step.
LEVEL C · Noisy Aer
Backend-calibrated emulator
Aer with a noise model from the live ibm_fez calibration. Predicts real-device behaviour before any QPU time is spent, and shows circuit and shot-budget issues offline.
LEVEL D · Real QPU
ibm_fez (156-qubit Heron r2)
Real superconducting hardware. One pair (test row, reference row) is one circuit, at 4,096 shots. Runs only after Levels A–C all pass and with explicit per-dataset operator approval. Not yet run.
LEVEL E · Score equivalence
Headline on real hardware
The tuned circuits of all three phases run frozen on the quantum processor and are compared with NumPy. Produces QAD PR-AUC and ROC-AUC on real hardware. Success: PR-AUC within 5% of the NumPy baseline and ρ ≥ 0.85. Not yet run.
LEVEL F · Sign-off
Backend-agreement report
A per-dataset brief: queue, circuit count, shot use, 4-way agreement matrix, score-distribution overlay, headline PR-AUC and deployment recommendation. Not yet written.
Status: Levels A to C wait for a final tuned configuration, which does not exist yet because tuning is still running. Levels D to F wait for Levels A to C. No QPU result is shown on this page because none exists.
